title: A Rare Case of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy with Subendocardial Late Gadolinium Enhancement in an Apical Aneurysm with Thrombus
case_prompt: A 71-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, general malaise, and bilateral lower‐limb edema. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or familial cardiac disease. On admission, he was in atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response and a complete right bundle branch block; there was no low voltage on ECG. Laboratory tests showed a B-type natriuretic peptide level of 1272.6 pg/mL (normal < 18.4 pg/mL), troponin I of 0.491 ng/mL (normal < 0.045 ng/mL), a white blood cell count of 5830/µL with 1.5% eosinophils, and a C-reactive protein level of 0.48 mg/dL. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a thin-walled, akinetic apical region with thrombus, hypokinesis of the basal and mid–left ventricle, an ejection fraction of 37%, left ventricular diastolic and systolic diameters of 49 mm and 39 mm, posterior and septal wall thicknesses of 12 mm and 17 mm, and a right ventricular free‐wall thickness of 10 mm; there was no left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, or aortic valve disease. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a thin‐walled apical aneurysm with subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement involving the mid-to-apical left ventricle and a smaller area in the right ventricle, additional subendocardial enhancement in the basal lateral wall, and midmyocardial enhancement in the markedly thickened basal interventricular septum. Coronary angiography demonstrated no stenosis or myocardial bridging. Endomyocardial biopsy specimens from the right ventricular septum revealed thickened fibrous endomyocardium extending through all layers.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Myocardial infarction was excluded because “coronary angiography did not show coronary stenosis or myocardial bridging.”  
2. Vasospastic angina or coronary thrombosis with atrial fibrillation was ruled out as “diffuse hypokinesis of the proximal portion and LGE involving a large territory of the mid-to-apex region of the LV ruled out this diagnosis.”  
3. Endomyocardial fibrosis was considered given the subendocardial LGE pattern, but “The most important features for the diagnosis of endomyocardial fibrosis are a reduction in longitudinal diameter and obliteration of the apex with normal-size LV ... hypereosinophilia is found in up to 30% of patients ... although this was not observed in the present case.”  
4. Amyloid light-chain amyloidosis was considered, yet “Multiorgan disorders ... low voltage on an electrocardiogram ... and speckled sparkling signs on echocardiography are frequently observed in amyloid light-chain amyloidosis, but there were no such findings in our case.”  
5. Sarcoidosis was acknowledged as a possible cause of subendocardial LGE: “advanced amyloidosis and sarcoidosis can also cause subendocardial LGE and should be considered as differential diagnoses, depending on the clinical context.”  
6. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was supported by the finding that “the markedly thickened bilateral ventricular walls and asymmetrical hypertrophy of the LV in the absence of another disease capable of producing hypertrophy ... were consistent with a diagnosis of HCM.”
